## Hallway Analysis

The curved motion could confuse or discomfort someone nearby because the robot is continuously changing direction while moving forward, making its movement unpredictable than straight motion. I would reduce the angular velocity to make the turn more gradual. The trade off is that the robot would need more time and distance to complete the same distance.

One safety criterion for acceptable motion around people would be maintaining a minimum passing distance, such as at least 1 meter from a person. This could be evaluated by recording the robot's and person's positions during a trial and measuring the minimum distance between them. The motion could be considered okay if the robot maintains at least the required distance throughout the entire movement and gives the person enough time to respond.

## Trial Synthesis

The three trials mostly matched what I expected. Trial 1 moved straight, so the robot stayed on a straight path. Trial 2 turned and then drove straight, which somewhat matched my prediction. Trial 3 moved forward while turning left, so it followed a curved path as expected but it did not move forward. 

The biggest difference was in Trial 3. I predicted the heading would change by 1.60 radians, but the odometry measured 0.967 radians. The difference was -0.633 radians. One possible cause is that the robot did not move at the exact commanded speed and turning rate for the whole 4 seconds. The path length was also shorter than predicted. To check this, I could compare the commanded speeds with the actual speeds recorded by the odometry.

If the robot moved straight at 0.15 m/s for twice the time, or 8 seconds, it would travel:

d = vt = 0.15 × 8 = 1.20 m.

So the predicted distance would be 1.20 meters.
